turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, sorry, I'm a bit late. The Victoria line just sat in a tunnel and I was stood there thinking, brilliant, this is all I need today.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a problem at all. Come and sit down. Can I get you some water?

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, I'm alright, thanks. Mouth's a bit dry but I'll survive. My partner Jamie rang you this morning, they were in a complete flap, made it sound like I'd collapsed on the platform or something.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception did pass a note along. I want it in your words, though. What actually happened?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, so, yesterday evening, train home from work, packed as usual, and out of nowhere my chest went really tight. I honestly thought I was having a heart attack.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): That sounds horrible. What else did you notice while it was going on?

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): I started shaking, proper trembling, hands and legs. And this huge wave of fear, I was sure I was going to die right there by the doors. Everyone else was just on their phones, which, you know.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. How long did it last, roughly?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, felt like hours. I reckon about ten minutes, then it eased off around Stockwell. I got off and sat on a bench like a lemon.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your partner said you looked pale and very frightened when you got home. Were you short of breath?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No, breathing was fine. I wasn't gasping or anything.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did the tightness spread into your arm, or up to your jaw?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Just a band across the middle of my chest.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any nausea, or were you actually sick?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Tummy was fine. I'd had a Pret sandwich at lunch, the chicken one, and a coffee that was honestly undrinkable, far too bitter, but that's not the point.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever blacked out, or had a turn like this before?

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Never blacked out. First time for all of this. I'm 26, I cycle to the station most days, I'm not exactly a heart attack candidate. Well, when it's not raining, so, never.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any medicines? Prescribed, or over the counter?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I barely take paracetamol. My sister's on setraline for her anxiety though, she's forever telling me to pinch one of hers. I didn't, obviously.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'm glad you left her tablets alone. Any heart trouble in the family?

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My dad's got high blood pressure. He's on ramipril, 5 milligrams, he rattles. Nobody's had a heart attack young, as far as I know. Oh, and he puts the remote in the fridge, but that's a separate issue.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke? And what about alcohol?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked. Alcohol, um, a couple of pints on a Friday if we make the pub. Jamie's the one who polishes off the wine.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work? Has anything been particularly stressful?

[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Bookshop, part time, and, err, a masters in the evenings. Deadlines are hideous, I've been up rewriting a chapter on Victorian drains. Dead romantic. The cat from next door sleeps in our window box, which is the real crisis.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check you over. Blood pressure is 122 over 78. Pulse is 96 and regular. Chest is clear, heart sounds are normal, and I can't hear any murmurs.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking back, when the chest was tight, were you actually struggling to breathe?

[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. I said I wasn't, but that's wrong. I couldn't get a proper breath, I was panting, and my hands went a bit numb round the edges. I just didn't want to sound dramatic on top of everything.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): That hand numbness often comes with over-breathing. Did you feel dizzy, or as if you might faint?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit lightheaded, yeah. I didn't go down, I stayed on my feet. Bloke next to me had these enormous headphones on, completely oblivious. Almost funny now.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you sweaty?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, clammy round the back of my neck. Not soaked. The carriage was roasting, mind you, someone had a coat on in June, unbelievable.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Day to day, tummy, bowels, waterworks, all ticking over?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, all normal, no bother. I eat pretty well, Jamie cooks, loads of veg, though I do raid the biscuit tin when I'm writing.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough or wheeze, or chest trouble the rest of the time?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): No cough, no wheeze. Chest is fine otherwise. I did briefly blame the coffee, then I remembered I've drunk worse.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you make of it, yourself?

[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I still reckon it was a heart attack, or the start of one. My uncle keeled over at 50 and everyone lost it, then it was just a pulled muscle from moving a sofa. Ridiculous story. I've been jabbing at my pulse every five minutes since, like a maniac.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can see why it frightened you. A young person, sudden tight chest with shaking, fear and fast breathing, on a crowded train, that pattern to me is a panic attack, not a heart attack. That's my working impression, not a stamped diagnosis.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't fully exclude a heart rhythm problem from the story alone, so I don't want to pretend I can.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok. That's, uh, nicer than I expected. Do I need tablets? My sister would be thrilled.

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No tablets from me today. I do want an ECG, a heart tracing, with the nurse straight after this, this afternoon. Lie still for it, and try not to chat through the recording, it only takes a few minutes.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll also book bloods for Thursday morning. Full blood count, kidney function and a thyroid check. No need to fast, just have your usual breakfast.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the ECG looks off, or if you have another episode before I see you, then we arrange a 24-hour heart monitor. Not today, only if one of those happens.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if things haven't settled, or those bloods come back borderline, we might do a chest x-ray. I won't book that now.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks with the results, whatever they show.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile, if it starts again, breathe in for four, hold for four, out for six. Practise that twice a day when you're calm, so you've got it on the train.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks, bloods Thursday, ECG in a minute. Got it. I'll try the breathing. Jamie's already made a spreadsheet, they'll be unbearable, but thanks, really.

spec.situation: Young adult after a first episode of sudden chest tightness, shaking and fear on a train; thinks it was a heart attack; no drugs; partner phones in details; doctor orders ECG, teaches breathing.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

omissions.text: Patient is taking no medicines at all, prescribed or over the counter, and specifically did not take sister's sertraline.

Family history recorded as sister having anxiety; transcript states sister is on sertraline for anxiety, but the clinically relevant family history additionally includes no known family history of a young heart attack.
Chest tightness was described as a band across the middle of the chest.
Initial denial of shortness of breath was corrected by the patient: during the episode they could not get a proper breath and were panting.
Negative finding: no actual fainting/syncope during the episode; patient stayed on their feet.
Negative finding: no cough or wheeze and chest fine otherwise the rest of the time.
